**Loyalty is a ledger** (decided 31 October 2026, build order item 17++; the owner: "Maybe make it a agnostic system? It grows towards who ever gives to them, and goes the other way for whoever takes from them? And starts not so high?", then "Agreed to all. Expertly."). The people of every province, and the men of every army, keep one ledger of what each actor has given them and taken from them, whoever he is: their king, his governor, a vassal, a rival king, a commander, a bandit chief. They follow whoever stands best with them. No role has a rule of its own.

- **A fair exchange is neutral.** What counts is what an actor takes against what he gives: protection (troops that defend them, policing that keeps bandits off, a siege lifted), grain in a famine, works built and light demands give; tax and levies beyond what that protection is worth, requisition, plunder, a sack and corvée unpaid take. A king who defends and taxes fairly holds steady; one who squeezes and gives nothing loses them. For an army, pay, plunder shared and victories give; wages unpaid, defeats and hunger take.
- **Credit goes to the hand they see.** Grain handed out by a governor earns the governor, unless it comes in the king's own name, by his envoy, his stela or his proclamation; so a governor who gives out his king's gifts as his own quietly builds a following, and a wary king gives in his own name.
- **Memory fades.** Recent deeds count for more than old ones; standing is earned again by every generation.
- **It starts low** for every newcomer: a new governor, a conqueror, a commander new to his men. Starting data can still say what history did: a native dynasty in its own land begins higher than an outsider, since it has given and taken there for generations; data, not a rule.
- **What follows from it, with no further rule:** a governor who turns takes only the provinces, and the levies, whose ledger stands better with him than with his king; the rest refuse him, rise against him or go their own way, and the king's standing garrisons stay the king's unless he has bought them; an army follows its commander only as far as its ledger stands with him; a conquered province's standing towards its new master starts low and rises as he gives, which is its absorption; and a province's unrest towards whoever holds it is how low its ledger stands with him, below ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"). The ledger is numbers under the hood, and no player ever sees them: a king learns where his people stand as he learns anything, from his governor, his spies and travellers, and how clearly depends on what he spends on knowing (the owner, 31 October 2026: "Under the hood, it will be a probability number, I imagine. But it should not be that tangible to a player. But the better you invest in information, the better resolution you get on the situation."): travellers' talk gives a vague mood for nothing, a governor's report is as honest as the governor, spies and envoys sharpen it, and a census gives the clearest picture, each dated as news is. First guesses for every weight, tuned in item 18.

**Whom a province obeys** (decided 31 October 2026, build order item 17++; the owner: "Can province ownership be made into something more agnostic? As in not something you owned hardcoded, but something that abides you, by a combination of force and loyalty?", then "Yes, please, expertly!"). A province is not owned by a flag: each season it obeys whoever it fears or loves most. Fear is force: troops standing in it or near enough to answer it, weighed against its own men of fighting age ("The people defend their land"). Love is the ledger: its standing with each actor who has given or taken there. The one whose weight is greatest holds it; if nobody's weight clears what its people will accept, it obeys no one and is lawless ("Land without a ruler"). Every way a province changes hands is this one rule seen from a side: conquest is force tipping it; revolt is love for another outweighing fear of the master when his troops leave or are beaten ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"); absorption is love growing behind the force; a governor turning is his standing outweighing his king's; succession is an heir inheriting only part of his father's standing ("A realm holds by its ledger"); and a ceded province obeys its new master only once his troops or his governor are there and he earns its standing, as cessions did. Obedience has degrees: a province held by a wide margin pays and levies in full, one held narrowly pays grudgingly and hides more ("The king says how much he wants" under The world), which the mood of the land shows ("Who holds what, and the mood of the land" under Interface). It does not flicker: standing and memory move slowly, the question is asked once a season, and a change of hands needs the new weight to exceed the old clearly; the seeded dice only settle exact ties at the margin. Every change of hands comes as news with its cause ("Gubla now answers to Aziru: his men stand at its gates, and Pharaoh has sent no grain in three years"). A change of hands is taken up, never thrust on anyone (decided 2 November 2026; the owner: "Also, in amarna letters, if loyalty can shift to anyone. Can someone who don't want the city get it? What if babylon hands a city to egypt in a peace settlement? Should the person also have to claim the settlement, or is it natural that the pharoh then has to subdue it, or that a city changes alligance to a character, which suddenly throws him in the middle of a power battle he wasn't planing?", then "Yes ro absolutely all pt these! Extra expertly expertly!"): a province whose weight tips toward someone declares for him, and obeys him only once he takes it up by an act of rule aimed at it, an order to take or hold it, a governor sent, a demand for its grain or men, or a letter accepting it; until then it stays with its old master, or is lawless if it has none. He may refuse it or leave it unanswered: the declaration stands only while the province still leans his way, and a refusal is an entry in its ledger against him, since a people turned away remember it. A cession by treaty is the same: the treaty gives the receiver the claim and binds the giver to withdraw, but the receiver still has to take it up, and its people still weigh him. So no one is pulled into a war he did not choose, but anyone may be handed a choice: a man offered Gubla in the middle of a struggle he never planned must decide whether to take it, as Pharaoh weighed the mayors of Canaan who wrote declaring their loyalty and begging for troops, and often left them unanswered. The man need not be there: a province declares for whomever its people favour most, wherever he stands, and the offer reaches him as anything does, never by itself ("Messengers are errands"; decided 2 November 2026, build order item 17++, issue #431; the owner: "Yes, expertly, if you think it is best.", then "Agreed, expertly. Though this is also information he can pass on or sell. I guess even just a rumor can spread? Maybe the town must be really into someone and have the means, if they commission a message and courier? And this is valuable information for the king of the land, or his enemies."). Word of a people leaning toward someone spreads as talk at the pace of the roads, bending as it travels, to him, to the king of the land and to his enemies alike, each of whom may act on it: the king with concessions, a governor or troops, his enemies by courting the claimant. Only a people far gone in his favour, with the gold to pay, commissions a message and a courier: the province hires like a city-state, from its people's purse ("Anyone can hire anyone"), any character taking the errand at his price; a character whose stakes it serves may carry it unpaid; and the claimant's own envoy or spy there reports it home. A courier knows whom he carries for and to whom, and may pass that on or sell it like anything he knows; one who is stopped, bought or never sets out means the offer never arrives, and it fades as the people's leaning does. One who takes it up from afar must still go, or send a man, to hold it. The lean that commissions a courier is a first guess, tuned in item 18. The ledger is the standing of the many: the provinces, their peoples and the rank and file of armies. Persons, kings, governors, vassals and every other character, do not obey a ledger but choose by their stakes, each playing to rank highest on the one scoreboard by the strategy his traits give him ("Stakes, not dispositions" under Characters): an agreeable man works from within the system, a bold one strikes out alone (the owner: "Remember that character's foremost motivation is always to rank higher on the scoreboard, so loyalty doesn't factor into it in the same way for a character's, as it does for a non-player entity like a province. But if it is a character with agreeable traits, then teh chosen strategy for maximizing their score standing is an more conservative one that favors working from within the system."). So the ledger decides what a person can do, which provinces and men would follow him, and his strategy decides what he will do. A vassal is the same rule one level up: his provinces obey him, and he serves his overlord by his oath for as long as his own reckoning says it pays. First guesses for every weight, the floor and the margin, tuned in item 18.

**Revolt follows conditions, not dice** (decided 20 October 2026; read through the ledger from item 17++, decided 31 October 2026, the owner: "Yes, fix all expertly!"). A province's unrest is how low its ledger stands with whoever holds it ("Loyalty is a ledger"): the ledger decides how far it leans away from him, and the moment decides when it rises, both from conditions the engine can see; the seeded dice only settle ties at the margin. The homeland too (decided 29 October 2026, build order item 17): land a power has fully absorbed starts loyal, its ledger long in credit, and needs far more to rise, so a home revolt is rare, but a king who keeps starving his own provinces can lose one. What decides it, each condition either an entry in the ledger or the moment:

- **How new the conquest is:** the ledger starts low with a new master and rises only as he gives, which is the land's absorption;
- **hardship:** famine or another catastrophe there, levies raised from it, gold taken from it, and troops taking its food, by how much they took, its own king's included (decided 29 October 2026), each an entry against whoever took;
- **the master's weakness:** his armies beaten, his capital besieged, his troops busy elsewhere: not an entry in the ledger but the moment, when a low standing becomes a rising;
- **distance:** far from the king, by the measure of item 7, since the people credit the hand they see;
- **a cause to rally to:** the province's old ruler alive and free, or a character of standing there who wants it, whose own ledger there may stand higher than the master's: the moment, and a man to lead it;
- **outside help:** a rival's gold, which enters the ledger as his giving, or his envoys and armies promising support, which make the moment; deniable like any bribe.

What holds it: whatever the holder gives, a good harvest left to the people, policing (item 15) that keeps its roads safe, and time, as old takings fade, all raising his standing; and troops in or next to the province, and a governor whose own standing there is high, which keep the moment from ripening. A province that revolts becomes a free power of its own, under its old ruler or the character who led it, with the levies it can raise, and one that revolts with nobody at its head is lawless ("Land without a ruler"); troops of the master in the province fight them as combat says. The owner does not see the number: he learns of unrest as he learns of anything, from his governor (who may misreport it), his spies and travellers, and sees it in the mood of the land ("Who holds what, and the mood of the land" under Interface). First guesses for every weight and the threshold, tuned in build order item 18.

**What is absent on purpose.** No war declarations, no truces, no alliance flags, no opinion meters. A power at peace is simply one nobody is attacking.
